question: The salt cedar along my riverbank is growing thick and spreading fast. What control methods could I use to manage it effectively?
answer: To effectively manage the thick and fast-spreading salt cedar (Tamarix ramosissima or T. parviflora) along your riverbank, a combination of control methods is recommended. Cultural control involves maintaining healthy riparian vegetative cover to compete with salt cedar. Mechanical control methods such as chainsaw cutting, bulldozing, mulching, and mowing can be used but must be combined with chemical treatments for effectiveness. Biological control includes the use of the saltcedar leaf beetle (Diorhabda elongata), which feeds on the foliage causing stem dieback. Chemical control options include herbicides like Triclopyr (Garlon 4) applied foliarly in late spring to early fall, cut-stump treatments anytime unless snow is present, and basal bark treatments anytime unless snow is present. Glyphosate (Rodeo) and Imazapyr (Arsenal or Habitat) are also effective with specific timing and application methods. Combining these methods will provide the best control of salt cedar along your riverbank.

question: I've seen salt cedar resprouting after cutting. What integrated control approaches work best in such cases?
answer: Salt Cedar (Tamarix ramosissima Ledeb. or T. parviflora DC.) is a perennial tall shrub or small tree that can resprout after cutting due to its deep taproot, extensive horizontal roots, and production of adventitious buds. To effectively control resprouting, an integrated approach combining mechanical and chemical methods is recommended. Mechanical control such as chainsaw cutting, bulldozing, mulching, and mowing must be combined with chemical treatments to prevent resprouting. Chemical control options include applying herbicides like Triclopyr (Garlon 4) as foliar spray (2-4 qt/acre) from late spring to early fall, cut-stump treatment (100% concentration) anytime unless snow is present, or basal bark treatment (1:3 herbicide to natural oil) anytime unless snow is present. Glyphosate (Rodeo) and Imazapyr (Arsenal or Habitat) are also effective when applied as cut-stump treatments. Additionally, biological control using the saltcedar leaf beetle (Diorhabda elongata) can feed on foliage causing stem dieback, which may aid in control over time. Maintaining healthy riparian vegetative cover (cultural control) is also advised to support ecosystem resilience.
